analysis.one_liner: Caps compensation for families injured by negligent pregnancy and women's health care and restricts related lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The Senate fell 11 votes short of the 60 needed just to begin debate on the bill, failing 49-44, and it never received an up-or-down vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created the first federal rules for medical malpractice lawsuits over pregnancy and women's health care. It capped pain-and-suffering damages at $250,000 per provider, cut awards by the value of any insurance the patient already had, made punitive damages nearly impossible to win, capped lawyers' fees, and blocked suits against doctors who prescribed FDA-approved drugs. It kept full compensation for measurable losses like medical bills and lost wages, and supporters — the bill cited doctors leaving obstetrics over insurance costs — argued it would keep maternity care available. Opponents said it would strip injured mothers and newborns of fair compensation and override state courts, and the Senate never got to debate it.
analysis.who_benefits: Obstetricians, hospitals, and malpractice insurers would gain the most: a federal ceiling on pain-and-suffering awards ($250,000 per provider, $500,000 total across institutions), shorter filing deadlines, new hurdles before punitive damages, protection from product liability suits over prescribed FDA-approved drugs, and a sliding cap on plaintiff lawyers' fees. Supporters argued pregnant women would also gain, on the theory that lower insurance costs would stop obstetricians from abandoning deliveries and reopen maternity wards — the bill cited claims that one in seven OB-GYNs had stopped practicing obstetrics. Patients who win lawsuits would keep full recovery of actual financial losses like medical bills and lost earnings.

how_it_helps.text: It capped pain-and-suffering damages at $250,000 per health care provider ($500,000 total across multiple institutions) in lawsuits over obstetric and gynecological care, while leaving compensation for actual financial losses — medical bills, lost earnings — unlimited.

It shortened the deadline for filing an obstetric malpractice lawsuit and required courts to sanction frivolous filings, and it let any party demand that large future-damage awards be paid out over time instead of all at once.

It barred plaintiffs from naming a doctor as a defendant in product liability suits over FDA-approved drugs or devices prescribed for approved uses, and it imposed a strict standard — deliberate intent to injure, proven by clear and convincing evidence — before punitive damages could even be sought.

It capped lawyer contingency fees on a sliding scale (40% of the first $50,000 down to 15% above $600,000) and required expert witnesses to practice in the same specialty as the defendant, provisions supporters said would filter out weak cases.

analysis.who_pays: Injured mothers and newborns: anyone winning a malpractice suit over obstetric or gynecological care would have pain-and-suffering awards capped at $250,000 per provider regardless of severity, awards reduced by insurance benefits already received, punitive damages available only for deliberate harm proven by clear and convincing evidence, and lawyer fees cut by a mandatory sliding scale — provisions that would reduce recoveries most for catastrophically injured infants whose losses are mostly suffering rather than lost wages. State courts would also lose their current rules, since the federal law would override state tort law in these cases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients injured by negligent maternity care

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages falls hardest on injured newborns: a baby with a birth injury may suffer a lifetime of pain and disability with modest lost wages, and the bill would cut off most of that compensation regardless of how severe the negligence was.

The bill required courts to reduce a patient's award by the value of benefits the patient's own health or disability insurance already paid, meaning patients who were insured would recover less and negligent providers would effectively be subsidized by the patient's coverage unless the insurer had a legal right to reimbursement.

Punitive damages — the penalty for the worst misconduct — would be available only for deliberate harm proven by clear and convincing evidence, with the jury never told the limit, making punishment for reckless malpractice essentially unreachable.

It was a federal override of state court rules: the bill preempted state law on damages, deadlines, fees, and evidence for obstetric malpractice cases nationwide, including in states that had chosen their own approaches.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had real appeal: it left economic damages fully recoverable, kept the right to sue intact, and targeted an access problem that the bill's own findings described as serious. But its costs fell on the people least able to bear them: babies injured at birth often live for decades with suffering that is real but hard to convert into lost wages, and the $250,000 cap on pain-and-suffering damages — set by Congress rather than a jury hearing the case — would bind those cases the most. The collateral source reduction could also let a negligent provider benefit from the patient's own health insurance. Proponents' premise — that damage caps lower malpractice premiums enough to bring back maternity care — was the justification for these trade-offs; the caps came first, and the access benefits were projected, not guaranteed. The bill also imposed a one-size federal rule on all state courts, preempting state tort law even in states that had not asked for it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill's supporters tried to bring it straight to the Senate floor, but a procedural vote that needed 60 senators to open debate failed 49-44, and the bill died there without ever being debated or voted on.

narrative.text: Sen. Rick Santorum introduced the bill on May 3, 2006 with 19 Republican cosponsors, including Majority Leader Bill Frist.
The bill moved onto the Senate calendar within two days, and a motion to proceed with a cloture petition was filed by May 5 — an unusually fast track to the floor.
On May 8, 2006, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 49-44, well short of the 60 votes needed: all 41 Democrats present voted no, joined by 3 Republicans, while 49 Republicans voted yes.
The bill never received floor debate or an up-or-down vote, and the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 with the bill dead.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients who retain the right to full jury-determined compensation for obstetric malpractice, and the plaintiffs' trial bar that represents them. Doctors, hospitals, and malpractice insurers did not get the federal caps they sought, and pregnant women in underserved areas got no new access measures either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients' right to full compensation; trial lawyers

sides.party_line_note: The cloture vote split almost perfectly by party: 49 of 55 Republicans voted yes while all 41 Democrats who voted opposed it, with only 3 Republicans crossing over.

industries.note: The bill put a hard federal ceiling on the largest and most unpredictable component of obstetric malpractice payouts — pain-and-suffering damages — directly limiting what insurers must pay on claims. Its gain came at the direct expense of injured patients' recoveries.

Caps, shorter filing deadlines, punitive-damage barriers, and shielding from product liability suits would lower doctors' malpractice exposure and premiums. Doctors argued this would keep them delivering babies; whether premiums actually fall enough to restore access in underserved areas was the central dispute the bill never got to answer.

Institutions got their own $250,000 cap per facility and a $500,000 total cap across multiple institutions, limiting their exposure when maternity wards were sued. The bill's findings tied this to keeping maternity wards open, but the immediate benefit was reduced liability payments.

Sliding-scale fee caps directly reduced the contingency fees lawyers could collect in obstetric cases, while damage caps, shorter deadlines, and expert-witness restrictions reduced the number and value of cases worth bringing. The plaintiffs' bar opposed the bill as part of a broader push for federal malpractice caps.

By barring doctors from being named as co-defendants in product liability suits over FDA-approved prescriptions, the bill removed one source of pressure on manufacturers in obstetric and gynecological drug cases. The shield applied to providers, not manufacturers directly, so the benefit was indirect.
